speechtext: I desire to call to the attention of the House to a state of things existing at present which I think should be remedied, and I may put a question to the House as a whole. A moment ago, in answer to a question on the Order Paper which was put to the Government, a statement was submitted which in the ordinary course ought to be incorporated in Hansard. The answer in question, however, was lengthy and the hon. member who had put it said he could dispense with the reading of it, and it was therefore made an order for return, and the return does not appear in Hansard. This procedure is not in accordance with the rule, which provides that when an answer is of any considerable length, the Speaker may, at the request of the Government, direct that it be made an order for return. When the order for return is tabled and an hon. member goes to the office of the Clerk who has the custody of these documents he finds that he cannot remove such an order from the office. If he wants to consult it-and this might very naturally take some time-he has to read it in that office. Is the House going to stand by this decision, that when a return is made to an order hon. members shall be deprived of the opportunity of properly studying it?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
The hon. member is
virtually entering into an argument, Which of course he cannot do on the Orders of the Day; nor can he put a question to the House on the Orders of the Day.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
Then, Mr. Speaker, I will submit the question to the Cabinet, or better still, to Your Honour, who is the proper authority in the circumstances. May I ask if it is the intention of Your Honour to
prevent hon. members from procuring, for their use and full examination, returns which are laid on the table of the House, without being constrained to sit in the office of the Clerk in order to obtain any information from the return which may be desired?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: The question which the hon. member has submitted to me is somewhat involved, and at the moment I can only answer in general terms. I shall make a more explicit statement on the point tomorrow. So far as I am aware, the practice which obtains in the office of the Clerk is precisely the same as that which has existed heretofore, and I am not cognizant oi any new instructions having been given to vary that practice. If the ordinary practice has been superseded by fresh instructions, such instructions must have been given without my knowledge, and I shall make ample inquiry into the matter and answer the hon. member more fully to-morrow.

speechtext:
The hon. member
would be quite in order, before the clause is finally adopted, in bringing up the question of this amendment for further discussion. I think it might be better, however, to obtain the unanimous consent of the committee to return immediately to subsection 1 for further discussion, and then, when that has been disposed of, return to subsection 3.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
Section 5 (a) subclause 1, as it appears in the Bill provides that there shall be a license fee to be fixed by regulation but not to exceed $25. This amendment, as contained in Hansard of last night, makes a very radical change in that provision of the Bill. As I understand the wording of the amendment, there is to be a fee for each exportation and importation of $5. Jf I properly understand

that provision, it means that for each particular importation there would require to be a special license issued for which there would be charged a fee of $5. That would mean that if a physician were to import $25, or $10 worth, or, in fact, any quantity of one of the drugs referred to in the section, he would have to apply to the department for a license and he would have to pay a fee of $5 for the license. That license would cover the particular transaction for which it was issued and if on The following day he wanted some other of the drugs referred to in the schedule, he would require to apply for another license and pay another fee of $5. The amendment provides for exemptions of the quantities of these drugs as set out in the Harrison Law, but it contains a provision that is not to be found in the Harrison Law, and that is with reference to the medication, aside from the narcotic drug itself. It says:
But every such remedy or preparation as is mentioned in this section must contain active medicinal drugs other than narcotics in sufficient proportion to confer upon the preparation or remedy valuable medicinal qualities other than those possessed by the narcotic drug alone.
This provision is not to be found in the Harrison Law, although the same principle has been adopted in the Treasury Orders under which the Harrison Law in the United States has been administered. What I would suggest is that this section should make provision for the manner of determining the medication aside from the narcotic drugs.
Under section 7A, subsection (1) of the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act which was amended last year, an advisory board was constituted for the purpose of considering the question of medication. It was primarily intended that it should deal with the question of medication of remedies which otherwise might violate the provisions of the temperance legislation in force in the different provinces. But the Act itself went further, and by paragraph (c) of subsection O) of section 7 delegated to the advisory board power to decide as to the medication of drugs in so far as they came within the schedule to that Act. I submit that there should be inserted in this clause a provision that the question of medication, aside from the narcotics, should be passed upon by the advisory board constituted under the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act. because otherwise we shall possibly have the administration of these two Acts' by different parties in the Department of Health, with a consequent lack of uniformity of decision on the question of medication. Section 6 of the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act provides :
The manufacture, importation or sale of all proprietary or patent medicines contained in

opium or its derivatives for internal use are prohibited.
If effect is given to the amendment we are now considering to the Opium and Drug Act, then to be consistent the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act will require to be amended to permit exactly the same proportions of narcotic drugs. There is no logical reason why we should permit the use under this Bill of limited quantities of narcotic drugs and prohibit the use of the same quantities of the same drugs under the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act. We would simply be in this position: The manufacturer of any patent or proprietary medicine could use the narcotic drugs by simply printing on the label or the wrapper a list of the ingredients.

The minister in introducing this legislation gave us a comprehensive and useful account of the international significance of the legislation as it related to the opium traffic; and as a matter possibly of historical and academic interest as to Canada's part in the suppression of that traffic, I may be permitted to add just a word or two to what the minister has said concerning previous legislation. The first time the subject came up in this House was following the riots which took place in Vancouver consequent on the Asiatic immigration. The Government was asked to compensate Japanese and Chinese for losses arising out of these riots. There were put in before the commission claims from Chinese merchants for losses sustained in connection with the opium traffic. Apparently at that time it was lawful to carry on the manufacture of opium in the province of British Columbia. A report was presented to Parliament on the losses sustained by Chinese in Vancouver, and that report is 74-F of the 1908 sessional reports. At page 15 a reference is made to the manufacture carried on by two opium manufacturers in Vancouver, one concern having a net profit in 1907 of $20,000 and the other a profit of $15,000. When this extensive manufacturing of opium came to the attention of the Government it was thought wise to investigate with a view to the suppression of the opium traffic. As I had personally to do with the first investigation, it became my duty to look into the question of the suppression of the traffic.
I preferred a report which was presented to Parliament in 1908 and which appears as report No. 36 B of that year. That report was followed by legislation introduced by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) 7-8 Edward VII, chapter 50, "an Act to prohibit the importation, manufacture and sale of opium for other than medicinal purposes." Then came the commission at Shanghai and at that commission a report which appears in the proceedings of the Shanghai commission, was presented on opium and morphia in Canada. It says that during five years from 1904 to 1908 there were imported of all grades of opium into Canada a total of 1,290,688 pounds. That was the significant feature of that particular report. Subsequent to that report came the legislation passed in 1911 for the suppression of opium and habit forming

drugs. The minister has dealt with the other features of the traffic. It occurred to me that possibly to students of this particular movement for the suppression of the opium traffic a reference to this data might be of some service.

speakeroldname: Mr. JACQUES BUREAU (Three Rivers and St. Maurice):
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: I think the Minister of Finance ought to give some explanation about the principle of this Bill. If I understand rightly loan companies, under the old Act, were obliged to make a return to the minister showing their financial condition, and if the minister was not satisfied with the statement he applied to the Treasury Board to appoint an inspector to look into the affairs of the company. It is mow proposed to make a change whereby the Superintendent of Insurance will make an inspection and report to the minister. The other powers of the Superintendent of Insurance are not increased, but the responsibility which heretofore rested on the Treasury Board will hereafter be vested in the minister, and the appointment of an inspector which was heretofore made by the Treasury Board will now be made by the Superintendent of Insurance. I would like the minister to explain why the change is made and what causes have brought it about. I understand that power is given by the Bill to even suspend the operations of a company if that company's financial statement is not such as to protect the shareholders or those dealing with the company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
The change
that is made in the law is to place loan and trust companies-because there is another Bill on the Order Paper dealing with trust companies-on exactly the same footing. The whole idea of the legislation in both instances is to place loan and trust companies in the same position that insurance companies are in at the present time. We have a regular and proper inspection of insurance companies, but there is no such inspection of loan companies or of trust companies. Perhaps I had better read the section in the Act as it formerly stood which deals with this matter:
The Treasury Board upon the report of the minister may appoint some competent person as inspector to investigate the affairs and management of the company, who shall report thereon to the minister. The Treasury Board may also prescribe the manner and the extent to which the investigation shall be conducted.
The House will observe that a special ,investigation is to be made only when the

minister requests it, and on his request the Treasury Board may grant that inspection. The old section went on to say:
It shall be the duty of all officers and agents of the company to produce for the examination of any such inspector all books and documents in their custody or power-
And so on, in order that the inspection may be expedited. As matters worked out that really meant that there was no inspection at all. Of course ordinarily there is nothing to draw conditions to the minister's attention; and anything which would indicate that an inspection of any particular company is necessary would not transpire until the harm has been done. The situation in connection with insurance companies is very different, because in the case of those companies properly qualified inspectors, as a matter of departmental routine, make an annual inspection; and if anything improper develops as a result of those inspections, or if there is any necessity for a special investigation, that necessity at once becomes apparent and the special investigation is held. The new section simply puts the loan and trust companies in the same position as insurance companies.
As to the matter which my hon. friend has pointed out, the suspension of a license or the giving of a limiting license, that-provision also is taken from the Insurance Act, and of course its object is perfectly clear to hon. gentlemen. If it is found that the affairs of the company are in such condition that it ought not to continue to be allowed to do business or to receive further public moneys-that the public ought to be protected from its operations-it stops. On the other hand, if the business of the company is getting into a position where it requires special inspection with a possibility 

perhaps, a probability-that the company cannot pull through, instead of giving the license for the year, the license is given again following the practice in the Insurance Act-for a limited period.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
The effect might be to
declare the company insolvent also.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
Under the
Winding-Up Act. The effect under that Act would be to allow the winding-up provisions to apply.
Motion agred to, and Bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-Definition-"Superintendent".

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
I see that the Superintendent of Insurance and his staff are to
perform the duties of inspection not only of insurance companies but also of loan and trust companies. Is it the intention of the minister to designate some special person to make the inspections of loan and trust companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
It is not expected that it will be necessary to make any special provision. Altogether we have now only some thirty trust and loan companies to be looked after under this Act, and they are comparatively small in their operations.
It may be necessary perhaps to get a little more clerical help, but at the present time we expect to be able to look after the work with the existing organization.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 2-Examination and report on condition of company, etc.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
I notice that this section involves a radical change in the law. Under the old Act the minister made the recommendation to the Treasury Board, and that board appointed the inspector. To-day, we as a Parliament give power to the superintendent and he directs any one of his staff to inquire into the business of these companies. I do not think that is a move forward. Of course, the superintendent reports back to the minister, but it seems to me that the minister, or, if he does not want to assume the responsibility, the Governor in Council ought to have the power to appoint the man who shall make these inspections if the superintendent himself does not make them. Here we are delegating power that heretofore rested in the Treasury Board, and that board acted upon the recommendation of the minister.
I do not object to the inspector making the report to the minister, and the minister taking action upon that report, but I do not think Parliament should appoint a superintendent of insurance, whoever he may be, to be the man to choose the inspectors who will investigate and report. Because, after all, their reports will be the only evidence the minister will have upon which to determine his course of action.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
We already have what has proved to be a very efficient organization to look after a very much more difficult business, having regard to investments. insurance ratios, and the like, than this business, and we are pimply applying existing machinery that has been tried and found sufficient. The superintendent of insurance has proved himself to be well versed in this kind of work, and is, I think,

in a very much better position to say what examination should take place than any minister, because the superintendent is thoroughly cognizant of the details of the business and is charged with full responsibility. I think the hon. gentleman will find that this section as drawn will work out perfectly well.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: But it comes back to the general system established by this Government of appointing commissions-we won't discuss that subject now-and such commissions must be responsible. But this amendment in effect says that Parliament is to appoint the superintendent of insurance as the man who shall delegate his representative to make inspections. We all know that it will be impossible for the superintendent himself to personally inspect all our loan, trust and insurance companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: May I draw the attention of the hon. member to the fact that at one time there was a good deal of difficulty regarding our insurance companies, but I do not think there has been any since the passing of the Act which was introduced by the hon. member for Queen's and Shelburne (Mr. Fielding). This is no new departure; we are simply adopting what has proved to he very satisfactory. The corresponding section of the Insurance Act provides that the superintendent of insurance shall visit personally, or cause a duly qualified member of his staff to visit, at least once in each year, the head office of each company. This amendment is merely applying what has been proved to work out excellently in connection with the insurance business.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
It is hardly correct for my hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) to say that the superintendent can appoint anybody to make inspections under the Act; he must appoint one of his own staff, who are public officials appointed in the same way as all other such officials.' The difference between this and the existing law is that under the existing law there might be inspection on any occasion when attention was drawn to some suspicious circumstances in connection with companies of this class; but now with the larger number of companies and with more public attention drawn to their operations, the hon. minister says: Instead of having an occasional inspection we will have one annually, and rather than create a new position I am going to make the present staff of the superintendent of insurance do [DOT] 
the work. I do not want my hon. friend from Three Rivers to give the minister a chance to appoint another man.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
But the microbe of extravagance is gradually crossing the floor of this House.
Mr. MoMASTER: If I mistake not, banks have to supply certain information to the Government month by month. I would ask the minister whether he has considered the advisability-apparently from this Bill he has not- of placing trust companies under similar obligations. Of course, there is certain information about notes and that sort of thing which trust companies could not give. But I rather think that the business of trust companies comes nearer to that of the banks than it does to that of insurance companies, and I would like to hear the minister's view as to the wisdom of assimilating the returns and reports required from trust companies to those required from banks and of insisting upon the same requirements concerning audits and so on in each case. My feeling is that many trust companies merely transact banking business which, under the regulations, the banks with which they are associated are unable to perform.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
There is no
doubt that the banking regulations are very excellent regulations, and also that they cost a good deal of money. The returns are voluminous, by reason of the extent of the ramifications otf the banking business. The main operations of the trust companies consist in looking after the investment of trust funds; the larger amount of their investments is in first mortgages and approved bonds, municipal or governmental.
Their real assets and invest-
10 p.m. ments, therefore, are more like those of the insurance companies than like those of the banks. However,
I think my hon. friend will agree that we are now taking effective steps to extend our jurisdiction over trust companies and to provide adequate protection for the public.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
As I understand it, our general statute provides for an interest rates of five per cent only, but in most cases the loan companies charge a much higher rate than that. Very often if a man is behind in his payments he has to pay compound interest. If the company has an idea of (foreclosing they may hand the mortgage to counsel, and on that account an additional charge of $20 or $25 is laid against the man who borrowed the money

when it comes to settle up. These things are onerous to the poor man who has to borrow, and I suggest that close inspection be made of these transactions with a view to seeing that the conditions of the loan are not all one-sided, as is very often the case in connection with loans made on mortgage by loan companies.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 70A-special report where assets are deficient:

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: Some of the language of this section seems to be rather clumsy. I suggest that the words "be held to be unauthorized" be struck out and that the word "cease" be substituted therefor, so that the sentence will read, "and the company shall thereupon cease to transact further business. We can authorize a company to transact business, but I do not think that we have jurisdiction to "unauthorize" a company to transact business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: I agree.

Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.

Sir HENRY DRAYTON (Minister of Finance) moved that Bill No. 58, to amend the Civil 'Service Insurance Act, be now read the second time.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-Authority to insure extended to persons in the navy:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: Will the minister explain how this differs from the old Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: We are increasing the maximum amount of insurance that can be carried from $5,000 to $10,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: This section is extending the benefits of the scheme to persons in the navy, which we are abolishing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
The old Act,
as I recollect it, applied only to civil and military employees. We are now extending it to the naval employees.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: There is no navy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: Oh, there will be a few persons.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
We are practically
being asked to vote money for naval officers who are not now on the strength; they have been dismissed. We are extending the benefits of the insurance scheme to a service which has just been abolished. I want to be logical. I want to know whether we are extending the Act to the naval service which has been abolished or to a new naval service that is to be created hereafter.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: Perhaps my colleague will allow me to answer that. The naval service has not been abolished. It is simply being reorganized and put on a more efficient basis. I shall have much more to say on this matter when the Naval Estimates are up.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: Are there any persons in the naval service who will come under this Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: The old Act did not extend to them. Is that the only change being made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries whether persons in the naval service would include not only those in the navy but the merchant marine, and those employed on dredges, tugs, and boats like the Lady Grey, the Montcalm, the Stanley, and other Government boats?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.

The object is to extend the benefits to all Civil Service em-

ployees. The old Act was not sufficiently broad in its terms, although as a matter of fact some Naval Department employees were eligible for insurance under this scheme.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
Then it would cover
those who are in the service of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: No. It extends only to civil servants and permanent officials of the militia and navy,

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: This section applies to those who were appointed to a permanent position in any branch of the public service after April 1, 1893. Why was the date fixed rather than any other?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: The Civil Service Insurance Act was passed in 1893. Up to 1914 the maximum amount of insurance that could be carried was $2,000, but the Act was amended in that year extending the maximum to $5,000. There has been no change since 1914.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: The minister did not catch my question. This section applies to all those who were appointed to permanent positions in any branch of the service after the 1st day of April, 1893. Why is that date fixed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: It takes in all employees who were appointed to permanent positions in any branch of the service after 1893. I cannot say at the moment why any one previously appointed should not be brought in, unless it has something to do with the age tables.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: What happens to the man in the service who, being under the impression that he is filling a permanent position, is removed from the service? Is he still entitled to insurance protection?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: Will the appropriations made by this Parliament cover all the employees who come under this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: Yes, that is the underlying idea.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Seotion agreed to.
On section 3-additional power to make regulations.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: What is the object of this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
The object is to enable the person insured to provide for

his dependents; the section provides that the money will not be frittered away. It will be paid in such a way that the dependents will get the full benefit of it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: Both this clause and the last are really intended to ensure the permanency of the service.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: This legislation really adds, without expense, to the attractiveness and the permanency of the service. The fund carries itself.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: I understand this to be akin to the ordinary insurance. I may confess to the minister that I do not know much about the matter. Does the man pay anything to the Government for the protection he gets? In an ordinary company he has to pay a premium and be subject to a health examination. When a man comes under this scheme is he also subject to such examination; does he contribute anything annually during his lifetime to the sustenance of the fund by way of a premium, and does any premium which he may pay bear any proportion to the amount for 'which he is insured?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: It does. The scheme is self-supporting; it is supported entirely by premiums received. It is run like an insurance company, but the premiums are somewhat lower than those in regular insurance companies. For example, a man in the Givil Service taking insurance at the age of forty-five pays monthly $2.13 per thousand for his insurance as against $2.63 in the ordinary company. The proof that the fund is selfsustaining lies in the fact that the reserve to-day is intact. The fund carried the insurance of the civil servants who went to the war and satisfied war claims to the extent of $151,000.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
Are they all death
claims?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: Yes,

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: Can the minister tell us what percentage of the civil servants have taken advantage of this scheme?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: I cannot say at the moment.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: The premiums are about 18 per cent less than in ordinary companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
I might cite
some figures to the hon. gentleman. A civil servant coming in at twenty pays per month *

86 cents per thousand, while the minimum rate in ordinary insurance companies is $1.19. The man of sixty pays $4.60 per thousand under this scheme as against $5.59 in outside companies. This is a cheap form of insurance, and it is possible to make it cheap because there are no expenses in connection with agents.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: Does this apply to the Outside Service?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
Yes.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speechtext:
On motion of Hon. S. Tolmie (Minister of Agriculture), the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
(Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Oleomargarine Act, 1919, Chapter twenty-four of the Statutes of 1919, second session, and to provide:
1. That section three of the said Act be amended so as to extend the time during which the manufacture In and importation of oleomargarine into Canada is permitted until the thirty-first day of August, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-one. and to extend the time during which the offering for sale, the sale, and the having in possession for sale of oleomargarine is permitted until the first day of March, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-two.
2. That section eight of the said Act be amended to provide that the Governor in Council may make regulations with respect to the importation, manufacture, inspection, marking, advertising and! sale of oleomargarine, and the seizure and confiscation of apparatus and materials used, or intended to be used, in the manufacture, treatment, or manipulation of oleomargarine in contravention of the said Act or of any regulation thereunder; and that such regulations may prescribe a penalty not exceeding fifty dollars recoverable upon summary conviction for the violation of any regulation made under the provisions of the said section.
3.	That section nine of the said Act be amended to provide that the penalty for violation of the provisions of the said section shall be enforcible upon summary conviction, and further that in no case shall the minimum penalty be less than fifty dollars.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: Explain;

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is
necessary to introduce this resolution asking for permission to bring in a Bill for the reason that the Act of 1919 remains in force only until August 31, 1920, in so far as the importation and manufacture of oleo are concerned. Permission is also given to have this material in possession until March, 1921. The object of the Bill will be to extend this privilege for the period of one year. Under section 8 of
the Act of 1919, the Governor in Council is permitted to make regulations respecting the importation, manufacture, sale, seizure and confiscation of apparatus, etc. To this we propose to add, marking and advertising. The application of the penalty of the old Act was from 25 cents per pound up to 50 cents per pound of oleo held illegally and a fine of not less than $10. This has been increased to not less than $50. Up to 1918 no oleo was permitted to be manufactured in, or imported into, this country. Legislation was necessary, or was considered necessary at that time, to permit both the manufacture and import, for the reason that butter was extremely high in price and fats were very scarce. We find that these conditions .still prevail, and there has been a strong demand from all over the country that the permission he extended for another year.
Oleomargarine is being used as a food in almost every part of the world. I do not know of any country at the present time that restricts its manufacture and use.
I think it is generally admitted that it possesses food value. It can never be considered to be equal to butter of good quality. However the best oleo is perhaps as good as some brands of butter that are sold in the market. There is no comparison as a spread for bread or use in other ways on the table between our best grades of butter and oleo, and oleo will never, in my opin- * ion, enter into competition with first-class dairy or creamery butter.
All oleo manufactured in the country is made under the closest possible inspection which is carried on in our packing houses under the Meat and Canned Foods Act, so that all ingredients aTe of good quality. One of the greatest objections to the sale of oleo in this country is its misrepresentation as butter when given to the consumer. It is proposed during tihe year to introduce such regulations as will make this much more difficult particularly in connection with the sale of oleo for butter in restaurants and similar places. Under the present Act it is necessary to hang up a card in any restaurant or hoarding house bearing the words "Oleomargarine served here." This is not always complied with, and it is the intention of the department to use every possible means to more carefully police the use of oleo than has been done in the past. .In addition to this, ithe increased fine will, I think, prove very useful in restricting the fraudulent traffic in oleomargarine. It is also proposed to have the word "oleo" printed directly into each package of oleomargarine sold.

At the present time we have two firms manufacturing oleo in Canada, the Harris Abattoir Company of Toronto, and the Swift Canadian Company with factories at Toronto, Winnipeg and Edmonton. The place occupied by oleomargarine in the commerce of the country is indicated by the following figures:
Pounds.
Oleomargarine manufactured in Canada to date since the Act came into
force	 18,358,046
Imported during three months to
March 31, 1918	 2,262,514
Imported during twelve months ending March 31, 1919	 4,217,916
Imported during ten months of 1920	5,237,803
Imported in February, 1920	 353,054
This shoiws that there has been a steady
increase in the quantity. A comparison of the prices of butter and oleo gives the following results:
Nine brands of butter, average 72.55c. lb. retail.
Fourteen brands animal oleo, average 44.21c. lb. retail.
Eleven brands vegetable oleo, average 39.27c. lb. retail.
The following is a statement of creamery butter manufactured in Canada:
Pounds.
1917		 87,526,939
1918		 93,266,876
1919		 98,903,686
showing that during the period in which oleo has been sold there has been a steady increase in the production of creamery butter. It is estimated as against this that the butter production in creameries and dairies during the year 1919 will have amounted to 223,903,686 pounds. It is quite apparent then that oleo so far has not injured the manufacture of butter or the butter business. When we take into consideration the high price of cows, the very high price of feeds used in the dairies, and the scarcity and high price of labour, it is not reasonable to expect that butter will be rapidly reduced in price. I might say also that there is a very stiff demand for the produce of the dairy, not only in the form of fresh milk but also in the form of condensed milk, cream and milk powder, as well as for the manufacture of ice cream and other such products.
Mr. OOCKSH'UTT: Could the minister give us the amount of duty collected on the oleomargarine imported?
Mr. TOLMilE: Oleomargarine is imported free, I understand. There are certain changes taking place in connection with the manufacture of oleo. While it has been largely manufactured from animal oils in the past, vegetable oils are now being used

to a very much greater extent, and most, or nearly all, of these are imported. It is expected by some of the experts whom I have consulted in connection with this matter that vegetable oils, being produced very much cheaper than animal oils, will ultimately take the place of the animal oils used in the manufacture of oleo.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: Could the minister give us any idea of the quantity of oleomargarine manufactured in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: The quantity manufactured in Canada since the Act came into force is 18,358,046 pounds.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: Do the component parts of oleomargarine come in duty free as well as the manufactured product?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: That is what I understand, at the present time. Now so far as the extension of time is concerned, it appears that the condition that prevailed when the Act was first passed to offset the high price of butter still obtains. Oleo is used to a very great extent by large numbers of poor people in the large cities and also in the country, and I consider that at the present time it is advisable to at least extend the Act for one year, and during that period to watch very carefully what measure might be adopted to put down the fraudulent use of oleo as butter. It is the intention of the department during that period to accumulate from other countries as much information as possible as to what is being done along this line, and to do their very best to apply this Act rigidly.

I do not believe there has been in Canada in the last quarter of a century any time when the press might be regarded as less reliable than it is at the present time.

speechtext: Since 1917.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
I feel.it my duty, Mr. Chairman, representing a constituency which is very deeply interested in dairying,

to protest against any further extension of the time for the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine. In entering this protest I have the support of the National Dairying Association of Canada-which comprises the provincial Dairymens' Associations of Ontario, Manitoba, Alberta, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island-the Fraser Valley Milk Producers' Association; the Milk Powder Manufacturers; the Canadian Creamery Association; the Milk Condensers; the Canadian Milk Distributors' Association, the Milk Shippers' Associations of the districts of Montreal and Bedford, Que.; the Dairymens' Association of the province of Quebec; the Dairymens' Association of Eastern and Western Ontario; and the Milk and Cream Producers' Association. In other words, the dairymen from one end of Canada to the other, and in every province of the Dominion, have placed themselves on record as opposed to a further continuation of the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine. They believe-and in my judgment have good reason to believe- that the use of this so-called substitute for butter will have a very bad effect upon dairying; and they have a right to ask that this House give special and favourable consideration to their appeal in regard to their industry-an industry which has hundreds of millions of dollars of capital invested in it, an industry which probably affects more people than any other industry in the Dominion that you could name; and an industry which pays out millions of dollars in one way or another, and is very closely associated with the progress and prosperity of agriculture in Canada.
I must say that I take exception to one reason given by the minister for continuing to allow the introduction into and the manufacture in Canada of oleomargarine. The reason given was the same as that embodied by the former Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Crerar) in the Order in Council of the 10th December, 1917, which permitted the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine. The statement then made by the minister as the reason for permitting this privilege was the scarcity of butter and of those fats which are essential to the upbuilding of a healthy body. I wish to submit, Mr. Chairman, that the reason given is not strictly in accordance with the facts as I understand them. That statement might have been based on very good grounds probably in the year 1915, because in that year-as the figures show-we did not produce a sufficient amount of butter in Canada to feed our own population, and
we had to import over a million pounds of butter in order to satisfy the needs of the Canadian people.
In 1916 the argument might also have been used, because in that year we fell behind in the butter needs of our people by about 800,000 pounds. But up to December 10, 1917, when the Order in Council was passed permitting the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine, the records show, we had produced not only a sufficient amount of butter to satisfy the needs of our own population but an exportable surplus of pretty nearly 7,000,000 pounds. So at that time there was no scarcity of butter and of those fats which it is claimed, and properly so, are essential to health.
It has also been claimed that another reason for this Order in Council was the high price of butter. Well, at the time the Order was passed on December 10, 1917, the price of butter was 40 cents a pound, and we permitted the importation of oleomargarinej which was sold at from 32 to 34 cents a pound. The argument therefore for permitting the introduction of oleomargarine was that our poor people could not find the other 6 cents to buy a pound of butter. I ask hon. members if they think that is in accordance with the facts? In 1917, it is true, the cost of living was rising, but there was plenty of work at high wages, and I ventured the assertion that there never was a time in the history of Canada when it was easier for the poor man to find the money necessary to buy a pound of butter than on the tenth of December, 1917.

speechtext:
Have you any record of
the export price of butter at that time?

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
I know the price of
butter on the date I mention was 40 cents a pound, and I presume that might be taken as a criterion of the price in other places. But the argument was that our poor people could not find the extra 6 cents a pound for butter; therefore they should be allowed to buy oleomargarine. If our poor people could not afford to pay 40 cents a pound for butter in 1917, how is it possible that they can to-day afford to pay 45 cents a pound for oleomargarine? That is the situation at the present time. What is the next move to be made if our poor people cannot afford to buy oleomargarine to provide the fats required for the proper nourishment of their bodies? Will an attempt be made to provide than with oils so that they may take their fats in liquid form?

I do not think there was any real ground foi the argument that there was a scarcity of butter in 1917, for our exports contradict such an argument; and it is not the case now, because our exports of butter from 1915 on to the present time have been increasing year by year, until last year we exported, in round numbers, something over
14,000,000 pounds. We cannot reasonably bring forward the plea of a scarcity of butter as a reason for allowing the continued importation and manufacture of oleomargarine. And in regard to the inability of the poor man to find the money necessary to buy a pound of butter in 1917 at 40 cents a pound, how can he find 45 cents a pound to-day to buy a pound of oleomargarine?

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: What was the production of butter for exportation in 1914 and 1915?

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: I will give the imports and exports. In 1914 our imports were 7,317,259, our exports 1,228,753; in 1915 our imports were 6,822,540, our exports 2,724,913; in 1916 our imports were 4,309,831, our exports 3,441,183 pounds.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
Is that an argument in
favour of free trade?

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
You can take it as
you like. It will be noticed from the figures I have given that our imports in each of those three years steadily decreased and our exports steadily increased. But in those three years our imports were greater than our exports, and showed that we did not produce enough butter to satisfy our home requirements. So the argument might have been put forward then that the scarcity of butter was a good reason for allowing the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine. But in 1917 our imports dropped from the millions to 922,335 pounds, while our exports increased to 7,990,435 pounds. So that in 1917 when this Order in Council was passed we had, as I have already stated, a surplus over and above our home requirements of about
7.000.	000 pounds, and we had to find purchasers for that surplus in some twenty world markets.
Since the Order in Council was passed, as the hon. minister has stated, we have manufactured over 18,000,000 pounds of oleomargarine and we have imported over
12.000.	000 pounds, and that is equivalent to saying that pretty nearly 30,500,000 pounds of oleomargarine have been used to replace the product of our dairymen.

If that figure is compared with the figures representing our exportation of butter, it will be found that the 30,500,000 pounds of oleomargarine has practically replaced about the same amount of butter and forced our dairymen to hunt all over God's creation to find a market for their surplus butter.
What reasons have been given for allowing the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine? No person would for a moment argue that we can build up the dairy industry by permitting the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine. The minister himself very properly says that you cannot regard oleomargarine as a substitute for first-class butter. I cannot conceive of any action more illogical than that of the Government in permitting the free importation into Canada of oleomargarine and of the fats and oils which enter into its manufacture. Every government since Confederation has recognized the right of Canadian dairymen to have a certain amount of protection, and every fiscal policy of all these governments has maintained a duty on butter imported into this country of four cents a pound. Is it logical to assume to protect the dairy interests by imposing a duty upon butter and at the same time to permit the free importation of oleomargarine for use as a substitute for butter? It is unfair; it is most unreasonable.
In the United States they have established a standard in respect of all oleomargarine manufactured in that country. The percentages of the ingredients must be as follows: oleo oil, 34.26 per cent; constituents of milk, 28.09 per cent; neutral lard, 16.27 per cent; cottonseed oil, 14.26 per cent; salt, 7.12 per cent. In Canada we have absolutely no standard, except that the oleomargarine must not contain more than 16 per cent of water. Moreover, we impose heavy penalties on any person who mixes some other substance with butter and then sells that article as butter. You may not mix oleomargarine with butter and sell the article as butter; you are liable to a heavy penalty if you do. But you may mix all the butter you like with oleomargarine; "there is no restriction so far as that is concerned. A few days ago it was stated in the House that fifteen or sixteen people had been fined for selling oleomargarine as butter, most of the prosecutions having been taken during the last twelve months.
I see in that list the name of one person from my section of the country who bad

been selling from 150 to 200 pounds of oleomargarine every week to the unsuspecting public as butter. He was fined $50 for that fraud. But why should he be fined? If oleomargarine is just as good as butter, where is the contamination in mixing oleo with butter? Yet those who advocate the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine say it is just as good as butter. We take mighty good care to protect people who would not eat oleomargarine on a bet. If you have the money with which to buy butter, you want to be certain that you get good butter; therefore we take precautions to prevent any person from mixing with butter this stuff which is said to be just as good as butter, in order that we may be sure that the article which we buy as butter is butter and nothing else. But you can mix all the oleomargarine you like with butter.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: Does not the question of price enter into my hon. friend's argument?

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: I have referred to the question of price. It is true that the price of butter is higher than the price of oleomargarine, but I believe that for no article of food that goes on any man's table does he get as good value as that which he gets for the money that he pays for a pound of butter.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: My hon. friend does not quite catch my point. You do not rob the consumer by giving him a higher priced article along with the lower one; that is, by giving him butter along with his oleomargarine. But on the mere question of price you rob him if you give him oleomargarine along with butter.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
He is being robbed by the sale of this oleomargarine. Our experience here is the same as the experience of the United States and of every other country where this stuff has been used. There is a great temptation to the retailer who is handling this stuff to sell it as butter. The statistics show that out of an annual consumption of about 500,000,000 pounds of oleomargarine in the United States, only about 92,000,000 pounds were actually sold as oleomargarine; the rest was sold as butter. The oleo is coloured, a certain amount of cream or milk or butter is mixed with it, to give it the "creamy flavour" and the "butter taste," as they say in their advertisements. That is all done to deceive the public, and the public are deceived. A farmer comes along to his village grocer with ten pounds of good butter. The grocer buys the butter at 60 cents a pound and expects to sell it at 65. He sends an order to Harris' or to Swift's for 100 pounds of oleomargarine done up in bricks, looking like butter, flavoured so as to taste like butter; and he places that on his shelf alongside the butter that he got from the farmer. He has bought that oleo at a price which enables him to sell it at a price of 45 cents a pound. A customer comes in and asks for a pound of butter. If that dealer can sell to the customer one of these bricks of oleo at 65 cents, instead of 45 cents, and let him go away thinking it is butter, he has made a good, big profit. That has been done. There have already been prosecutions in the country. What for? Because people were doing that very thing. The authorities in the United States have done everything they could to try and stop it. They have put an excise tax of 10 cents a pound on coloured oleomargarine, and i of a cent a pound on the uncoloured. The idea was to protect the makers of butter, but it does not seem to have made that effect. There have been prosecutions by the score in the United States and in the Old Country, and we are getting them here in Canada. I really believe that in this country fully 50 per cent of the oleomargarine that is sold to the public is sold as butter, and at the price of butter. Talk about robbing the people ! Why is it that oleomargarine is selling from 40 to 45 cents a pound in Canada, while you can buy it in England at 26 cents? Are they losing money on it in the Old Country at 26 cents? I do not think so. If they are not losing money on it at that price, it is clear that the people here are taking 14 cents more per pound out of the pockets of the public than they should take. The whole thing is in the interests of one or two people who are manufacturing this stuff, and of those who live in tropical countries and are interested in the sale ol these vegetable oils.
Referring again to the argument that the importation of oleomargarine was permitted because butter was scarce and high in price in this country, I have already said that the Order in Council was put through on the 10th of December, 1917. The price of butter at that time was 40 cents a pound. On January 21, 1918, the price was 44i cents, on the 4th of March 471 cents, and on the 26th of March 49 cents. These figures were quoted by the hon. member (Mr. Crerar) to indicate that notwithstanding the Order in Council permitting the

importation of oleomargarine, the price of butter had increased. The price of butter went up a little as it always does at that season of the year. Oleomargarine at that time was selling at from 32 to 34 cents. In the month of October, 1917, butter was selling at 45 cents, in November it dropped to 41 cents, and in December was down to 40 cents. Why? Because the cheese factories had closed, and there was a greater amount of milk going into the manufacture of butter. That happens every year. No [DOT] person will claim, I think, that a farmer or a dairyman would make as much money selling butter at 49 cents in March as he would make selling it at 41 cents in November.
I have given some figures on the importation and exportation of butter showing that we have a surplus of that article in this country. Taking the stocks of dairy produce in Montreal and comparing the 31st of March of this year with the 31st of March last year, we find that there was held dn stock at Montreal, ready for export I presume, 6,780 packages of butter last year as compared with 24,383 packages this year. That shows that our dairymen are experiencing some difficulty in finding ready markets for their surplus product, which accounts for these stocks accumulating, and the figures indicate very clearly that they are accumulating.
I do not know why this favour should be granted to these people who are interested in the manufacture o,f oleomargarine -because it is a favour to them. It is a favour to the manufacturers who are making large sums of money out of it, and a favour of these people who are interested in the sale of these vegetable oils which enter into the manufacture of oleomargarine. The United States last year obtained a revenue of over- 81,250,000 from their tax on oleomargarine. We obtained nothing, because we had no taxation on it in any shape or form. I do not think there is anything which has so great a bearing on the prosperity of the farmer as the keeping of cattle. A farmer to be prosperous must maintain the fertility of his soil, and the keeping of cattle has that effect. I do not think any person who gives the matter any study can claim, having regard to the capital invested, and the amount of time and labour expended in the production of butter, that the farmers or dairymen are getting too high a price for their butter today. It can be easily shown, and has been shown in this House on former occasions, that from the standpoint of food value but-

ter at 65 cents a pound is a very much cheaper article of food than beefsteak at 35 cents a pound.

speechtext:
I have every respect for the Minister of Agriculture, and I can thoroughly appreciate the reasons actuating him and the Government in proposing an extension of time. I said at the beginning of my remarks that I believed there were a large number of people in this country who were asking for the continuation of this privilege, and evidently the Minister of Agriculture and the Government think so, or they would ' not be taking the steps they are taking. But the people of my constituency and the dairymen of this country, and a large number of my constituents are interested in the dairy business, are opposed to the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine, and I am here to represent the dairymen and farmers of the county of Frontenac. That I propose to do. Whether my view prevails or not is another question. I shall at all events do what I consider to be my duty.
I am somewhat surprised at the attitude taken by some members who come from city constituencies. It is probably true that quite a number of hon. gentlemen living in those constituencies want to have the privilege of buying oleomargarine, but we have hon. members who are very deeply interested in certain lines of manufacture. Those hon. gentlemen come mostly from city constituencies and the plea they put forward is the great item of expenditure which the poor man has to face if he wants to have butter. They say that he is not able to raise money to buy butter, and it grieves their souls to think that the poor man should be so circumstanced. They therefore

say that as he cannot afford to buy butter he ought to be allowed to buy oleomargarine, which costs much less. With great disinterestedness they base their arguments on the poor man's necessity. If we were to propose to some of these same gentlemen who are interested in certain lines of manufacture the removal of the protection which is granted to their particular industries, and to suggest that they should come into competition with producers of cheaper articles throughout the world, there would not, I imagine, be so much consideration for the poor man then. And yet I might argue, from the standpoint of the farmers of' the county of Frontenac, that perhaps we might reduce the amount which city people have to pay for certain manufactured articles, and thereby save to them enough money to enable them to buy farmer's butter. I might legitimately use that argument, and I therefore throw out this hint to hon. gentlemen who come from city constituencies-

Yes, my hon. friend
from Brantfdrd (Mr. Cockshutt) is one of them. speechtext: That is a good threat.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext: Very well, you may take it as a threat if you wish, and I shall not quarrel with you.

speechtext: You are making for a fight.

maintopic: STATUS OF QUESTIONS PASSED AS RETURNS.
speechtext:
If I am making for a
fight, I suppose my hon. friend, who is of a kindly disposition, will accommodate me; I would be surprised if he would not. I want to say before I conclude that in my judgment the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine was a mistake from the very first. It never should have been permitted, and it should not be allowed to rontinue at the present time. Other countries like Sweden and Australia are taking special steps to protect their dairy and allied industries, and in Sweden the dairymen are urging the Government to pass special legislation to protect their industries. I therefore think it unfair to the farmers and dairy-114
men of Canada that they should be obliged to submit to having their own product driven out of the country and forced to seek markets all over the world. I do not think hon. gentlemen who come from city constituencies, like, my hon. friend from Brantford, really appreciate the fact that the dairymen and farmers of the country have invested millions of dollars in building barns and stables and have to attend to their stock for five or six months in the year before they can get returns; nor do I think they appreciate the amount of time, labour and skill expended in the dairy industry. If they did, their attitude in this matter would be different. I can of course only protest as one member against the further extension of time in regard to the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine, and I do so believing that I am only discharging my duty to my constituents.
